title: Irrigation Flow Volume Calculator
description: Convert flow rate and run time into total water volume with the Irrigation Flow Volume Calculator — gallons, litres and acre-inches. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a zone flowing at 20 gallons per minute for 90 minutes delivers exactly 1,800 gallons (about 6,814 litres) — the tank drawdown, computed before it surprises anyone.
quick_answer: The Irrigation Flow Volume Calculator multiplies a system's flow rate by its run time and returns the total water delivered, in gallons and litres. Enter gallons per minute and minutes and read the volume — for tank checks, session comparisons and spotting the zone that drinks more than its neighbours.

body.t: Will the tank survive tonight's schedule? Sum the sessions' volumes here before the pump answers the question at 3 a.m.
Zones on the same controller should deliver comparable volumes for comparable areas. The outlier zone this arithmetic exposes is usually a leak, a stuck valve or a design debt.

Farm water is ordered in acre-inches. Converting a pump's gallons into acre-inches (÷ 27,154) puts well, pump and crop on one page.
20 gpm × 90 min = 1,800 gallons ≈ 6,813.7 litres. Spread over the 5,027 sq ft of a 40 ft sprinkler circle, that is about 0.57 inches of water — the depth figure growers actually manage by.
500 gpm for 2 hours = 60,000 gallons ÷ 27,154 ≈ 2.21 acre-inches. Two hours of that pump is a meaningful slice of a field's weekly water — now it is a number, not a feeling.

faq: Total volume from flow rate and time: gallons per minute × minutes = gallons, with litres and acre-inches alongside.
The multiplication is exact; the flow is the estimate. A system's true gpm varies with pressure and simultaneous zones — measure yours once and the calculator becomes precise for your system.
No. Flow and time in, volume out.
The water that covers one acre one inch deep: 27,154 gallons. It is the unit wells, water rights and farm irrigation are planned in across much of the US.
Metric systems rate in L/s: multiply by 60 for L/min, and the same volume logic follows. A 2 L/s line for an hour delivers 7,200 litres.
How deep is the water on my area?
Volume ÷ area: 1,800 gallons over 5,027 sq ft is about 0.57 inches (using 1 inch over 1 sq ft ≈ 0.623 gallons). Depth is the figure plants experience.
Indirectly: if a zone's computed volume at its known flow and time keeps exceeding what its area should need, the water is going somewhere — that comparison is the leak hunt's first step.
How do I find my system's real flow?
Time a meter reading over a known run, or catch a zone's output: volume ÷ minutes is your gpm. One measurement makes every later calculation yours instead of the brochure's.
Two zones run together — total volume?
Add their flows, then multiply by the shared run time. Combined flow is also the figure that tests whether the supply can hold pressure.
